claims.claim: Settled: licensing-monetization.md is right and monetization.md is wrong. Shipping the closed Play Billing Library in the same APK as onionhoney's ported GPL-3.0 code needs a GPL s.7 additional permission from the copyright holder of that code. It is a legal requirement, not a courtesy. monetization.md's precedents don't show otherwise: Thunderbird for Android is Apache-2.0, and Twisty Timer and Tasks.org ship billing with other people's GPL code and no exception. They show tolerance, not permission (see billing-15 to billing-17).

Play Billing is not a GPL 'System Library'. GPL s.1 limits System Libraries to things 'included in the normal form of packaging a Major Component' (kernel, window system, compiler or interpreter) that serve 'only to enable use of the work with that Major Component, or to implement a Standard Interface' with a public-source implementation. The billing client is a Maven artifact that each app bundles. It ships with neither the OS nor a compiler, and its job is to talk to the Play Store app. The FSF FAQ also says libraries 'can only qualify as System Libraries as long as they're not distributed with the program itself' (#WindowsRuntimeAndGPL).

com.android.billingclient:billing 9.1.0, the latest release, declares 'Android Software Development Kit License' in its POM. It has no sources jar (HTTP 404). Its classes.jar holds 337 obfuscated classes under com/google/android/gms/internal/play_billing plus 269 in com/android/billingclient/api, and it is merged into the app's dex. Its manifest binds to com.android.vending.billing.InAppBillingService.BIND and needs minSdk 23 (Rouxtine's 24 is fine). It pulls in play-services-base, basement, location and tasks under the same SDK licence, plus Apache-2.0 datatransport and AndroidX. billing-ktx 9.1.0 is also under the SDK licence.

The Android SDK License Agreement grants a 'limited, worldwide, royalty-free, non-assignable, non-exclusive, and non-sublicensable license to use the SDK solely to develop applications' (s.3.1). It says 'you may not copy (except for backup purposes), modify, adapt, redistribute, decompile, reverse engineer, disassemble, or create derivative works of the SDK' (s.3.4), and Google 'reserves all rights not expressly granted' (s.3.3). Recipients of the APK therefore get neither source nor GPL freedoms for the library, which makes it GPL-incompatible.

Under the GPL text and the FSF's reading, the play APK is one combined work. FAQ #GPLStaticVsDynamic: linking 'statically or dynamically ... is making a combined work'. FAQ #MereAggregation: modules 'included in the same executable file ... are definitely combined', so the s.5 'aggregate' clause doesn't apply. s.5c requires licensing 'the whole of the work, and all its parts, regardless of how they are packaged' under the GPL. s.1 puts 'dynamically linked subprograms that the work is specifically designed to require' in the Corresponding Source, which s.6 obliges the distributor to provide, and nobody can provide the billing source. FAQ #GPLWrapper: putting a permissively licensed wrapper module in between is 'legally irrelevant'. No court ruling on Android linking was found; this is the FSF's interpretation.

Only the copyright holders can grant the fix, and the grant must cover the whole program. FAQ #GPLIncompatibleLibs: 'Only the copyright holders for the program can legally release their software under these terms ... you cannot authorize the exception for them. You have to get the approval of the copyright holders'. #LinkingOverControlledInterface says the same. s.7: if permissions cover 'only part of the Program ... the entire Program remains governed by this License without regard to the additional permissions'. Adding the exception to the owner's own files alone does nothing for an APK that also contains onionhoney's code. Anyone who conveys the work may strip the permission (s.7 para 2).

The permission doesn't have to arrive inside upstream's licence file. s.5c: the GPL 'does not invalidate such permission if you have separately received it', so a written reply in a GitHub issue or an email works. Once Rouxtine applies it, s.7 requires 'a statement of the additional terms' in the relevant source files 'or a notice indicating where to find' them, for example SPDX headers pointing to a LICENSE-EXCEPTION file.

The code Rouxtine ports has one copyright holder. AnkiDroid is not a billing precedent either. It is GPL-3.0 (COPYING), with an AGPL-3.0 backend and an LGPL-3.0 API, and it ships no Play Billing library: none appears in AnkiDroid/build.gradle.kts or gradle/libs.versions.toml at 9015ffb. Model exception texts exist. The FSF FAQ (#GPLIncompatibleLibs) gives a GPLv3 s.7 template: 'If you modify this Program, or any covered work, by linking or combining it with [name of library] (or a modified version of that library), containing parts covered by the terms of [name of library's license], the licensors of this Program grant you additional permission to convey the resulting work.' The FAQ says to drop the braced source sentence when the library's source can't be distributed, which is the case for Play Billing. SPDX publishes the same wording as GPL-3.0-linking-exception.

There is no way around the library on Play. The deprecation FAQ says: 'By Aug 31, 2026, all new apps and updates to existing apps must use Billing Library version 8 or later', which rules out a home-made AIDL client. Paid downloads need no library: 'Developers charging for app downloads from Google Play must use Google Play's billing system', and the store runs that checkout itself. Rights from a holder come back permanently if the holder doesn't notify within 60 days after the violation stops, or if it is the first notice from that holder and it is cured within 30 days. claims.claim: Play Console Android vitals needs no SDK. Data comes only from users who opted in to share usage and diagnostics data with Google, only from certified devices, and only for installs from Google Play. Installs from GitHub, Obtainium or F-Droid never appear. Data updates daily. Play Console keeps 90 days and the Play Developer Reporting API keeps three years. Bad-behaviour thresholds: user-perceived crash rate 1.09 % overall, ANR rate 0.47 %, and 8 % per phone model for both.

Inference: Android vitals data is collected by Android and Google Play, not transmitted by the app. It therefore needs no entry in Rouxtine's Data safety form and no in-app consent. Play's form covers data 'transmitted off a user's device from your app', including by libraries and SDKs.

ACRA 5.14.2 (Maven Central, updated 2026-10-01) is Apache-2.0, which the FSF and ASF say can go into GPLv3 projects, in one direction only. AAR minSdk is 14. acra-core (294 KB) plus acra-http (71 KB) add about 0.37 MB of artifacts before R8. Their only dependencies are kotlin-stdlib, androidx.annotation and auto-service-annotations, which the app already has or which cost nothing at runtime.

ACRA queues offline. Approved reports stay as files and are scheduled for sending again at each app start (StartupProcessorExecutor). SendingConductor sends them through every configured sender, a few per run.

ACRA senders: HttpSender sends with no user action but needs a backend. MailSender uses an ACTION_SEND_MULTIPLE intent, and the user must pick an email app and send the mail. Custom ReportSenders are allowed. The official backends are Acrarium (Apache-2.0, Spring Boot + Vaadin + MySQL, so it needs a server) and the unmaintained Acralyzer. The only hosted backend listed is the commercial Tracepot. Without a server, ACRA's no-cost paths are email or a custom sender, such as a pre-filled GitHub issue.

Two F-Droid precedents for ACRA carry no Tracking anti-feature. AnkiDroid ships ACRA (http, dialog, limiter) to a password-protected, self-hosted Acrarium, and its fdroiddata metadata lists no AntiFeatures. NewPipe ships acra-core 5.14.2 with its own error screen: the user can copy a Markdown report or, after a privacy-policy dialog, send it by email or open a GitHub issue. NewPipe's only anti-feature is NonFreeNet, for YouTube.

sentry-android-core 8.62.0 (2026-10-27) and its core jar io.sentry:sentry are MIT. The AAR declares minSdk 21. Measured added artifacts come to about 1.81 MB before R8: the sentry jar (1.28 MB), the core AAR (0.50 MB) and epitaph 0.1.1 (MIT, 31 KB). Its lifecycle and core dependencies are already in a Compose app. The meta-artifact io.sentry:sentry-android also pulls sentry-android-ndk with native libraries, which Rouxtine does not need.

Sentry Android queues offline by default. AndroidOptionsInitializer sets cacheDirPath to Context.getCacheDir()/sentry and installs AndroidEnvelopeCache. maxCacheItems defaults to 30 envelopes, and the oldest is deleted when the cache is full. Auto-init through SentryInitProvider can be turned off with the manifest meta-data io.sentry.auto-init=false, so the SDK can start only after consent.

What Sentry Android sends by default: a random installation ID whenever an event has no user ID (not controlled by the Data Collection options); device and OS context (manufacturer, model, memory and more); and IP address '{{auto}}', which the server infers, while dataCollection.userInfo is on. sendDefaultPii defaults to false and is deprecated. attachScreenshot and attachViewHierarchy default to false. The server-side setting that stops storing IP addresses does not stop geo extraction; removing geo data needs an Advanced Data Scrubbing rule.

Sentry SaaS EU region: error events, transactions, logs, release health, debug symbols and backups are stored at rest in Frankfurt. User accounts, organisation settings, project metadata, DSN keys, usage data and support interactions can stay in the US. The region cannot be changed after the organisation is created.

Sentry's free Developer plan: $0, 1 user, 5k errors, 30-day lookback, 50 replays, unlimited projects. The pricing table lists 'Data Residency' among plan features, and the extracted table implies the Developer plan includes it, but this was not confirmed in the docs.

Self-hosted Sentry is FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0 (source-available; each version becomes Apache-2.0 after two years, so it is not FLOSS at release). It needs 4 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM plus 16 GB swap, and 20 GB of disk. Without a server or budget, that rules it out.

A Sentry DSN is safe to publish: it 'only allow[s] submission of new events' and gives no read access. That matters for F-Droid, which 'does not sign up for any API keys' and includes any keys in both source and binary. The DSN, or a PostHog project key, must therefore be committed for F-Droid builds to report at all.

The PostHog Android SDK keeps its queue in device file storage and flushes it when the device is online. Defaults: maxQueueSize 1000 (oldest dropped first), flushAt 20, flushIntervalSeconds 30. Consent hooks: optOut=true in the config, PostHog.optIn() and optOut(). captureApplicationLifecycleEvents defaults to true. personProfiles defaults to IDENTIFIED_ONLY. Android error tracking needs errorTrackingConfig.autoCapture=true (default false), and R8 mapping upload is supported. The docs say nothing about ANR or native crash capture.

PostHog Cloud free tier each month: 1M analytics events, 100K error-tracking exceptions, 5K session recordings. It covers 1 project with 1-year retention, needs no credit card, and usage stops at the free limits instead of billing. PostHog Cloud EU is hosted in Frankfurt, IP data capture is off by default for new EU projects, and a DPA is available. The server repository is MIT except the ee/ directory.

PostHog's capture API makes a dependency-free client possible. The EU host is eu.i.posthog.com, with /i/v0/e/ for single events and /batch/ for batches (request body under 20 MB). Events need api_key, event and distinct_id. Adding '$process_person_profile': false keeps them anonymous, with no person profile. The endpoints are POST-only and return no sensitive data.

It keeps crash data 90 days and 'may process and store your data anywhere Google or its agents maintain facilities', so there is no EU residency. Google acts as processor under the DPST, SCCs and DPF. Opt-in works through firebase_crashlytics_collection_enabled=false plus setCrashlyticsCollectionEnabled(true). While collection is off, crashes are stored on the device and sent once collection is enabled. The service costs nothing.

It pulls Ktor client, kotlinx-serialization and AppCompat, measured at about 3.8 MB of artifacts before R8, not counting OkHttp. By default it caches signals on disk and keeps a generated user ID, which it double-hashes with a server-side salt. In its in-memory mode, unsent events are discarded when the app is killed.

No source was found saying the backend is open source. The live pricing page returned 404.

Aptabase fails the offline-first constraint. The Kotlin SDK's trackEvent POSTs each event at once on a thread pool and only logs IOExceptions, so it has no queue, and it does no crash reporting. The SDK moved to JitPack (0.1.0, minSdk 16); the last Maven Central release is 0.0.6 from May 2023. The server is AGPL-3.0. The hosted free plan gives 20,000 events a month with EU or US residency.

The server, Countly Lite, is AGPL-3.0 with a modified s.7 that forbids removing Countly branding, and needs your own server. The hosted Flex plan starts at $175 a month.

It stores up to 32 events on disk (maxPersistedEvents) and by default generates and persists an anonymous ID (generateAnonymousId). The SaaS is proprietary. The free plan gives 1 user, 7.5K events and 1M spans a month with 7-day retention. EU data residency could not be confirmed from a BugSnag page.

F-Droid's Inclusion Policy forbids proprietary tracking, ads and analytics libraries and asks for a FLOSS alternative or a build flavour without them. It allows prebuilt FLOSS binaries from Maven Central, Google Maven, JitPack and similar repositories, provided they are freely licensed. ACRA (Apache-2.0), Sentry, PostHog, Countly, Bugsnag and TelemetryDeck SDKs (MIT) all pass that test.

F-Droid's Tracking anti-feature is for apps that report activity 'without your permission or by default'. It is not applied 'if the functionality is opt-in (i.e. you are asked before it happens) and disabled by default', provided enabling it requires informed consent ('a privacy policy similar to GDPR') and collects as little personal data as possible. The one-line summary on the same page reads 'even when it can be turned off', so an opt-out design would be flagged. Apps tagged Tracking are hidden by default in the F-Droid client.

F-Droid defines NonFreeNet as 'promote or depend entirely on a proprietary network service'. Inference: optional crash reporting to sentry.io, whose server is FSL and not FLOSS at release, neither promotes it nor depends on it entirely, so it should not trigger the label, but labelling is reviewer discretion. Pointing the foss DSN at GlitchTip (MIT) removes the question. A 'Non-Free Dependencies' label does not apply because nothing proprietary must be installed.

F-Droid precedents for analytics SDKs in the F-Droid build. Element X's non-enterprise build includes the PostHog and Sentry analytics providers in every flavour, including fdroid, behind an opt-in prompt, with PostHog sent to Element's own posthog.element.io. Its fdroiddata metadata has no AntiFeatures. Tasks.org takes the other route: Firebase, Crashlytics and PostHog live only in its googleplay flavour, the F-Droid recipe sed-deletes gms and Crashlytics lines, and the generic build carries no anti-features.

Play Data safety rules. 'Collect' means transmitting data off the device, including by SDKs; data processed only on the device is not collection. Transfers to service providers processing on the developer's behalf are not 'sharing'. Data may be marked 'optional' only if every user, in every region, can opt in or out. Relevant data types: Crash logs (for example stack traces), Diagnostics (for example latency and battery), Other app performance data, App interactions (for example page visits), and Device or other IDs ('identifiers that relate to an individual device, browser or app'). Every app needs a privacy policy link.

Inference, Data safety entries for the recommended setup. Crash logs and Diagnostics: collected, optional, not shared, purpose Analytics, encrypted in transit. App interactions: the same, only if usage stats ship. Device or other IDs: only if a persistent per-install random ID is sent (Sentry's installation ID, a PostHog distinct_id). Approximate location: only if IP-derived geo is kept, so scrub Sentry geo and turn off PostHog GeoIP to avoid it. Also offer a deletion route (email).

EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of ePrivacy art. 5(3), v2.0, adopted 7 October 2024. Art. 5(3) covers 'any information ... regardless of whether or not it is personal data' (CJEU Planet49, C-673/17). Software on the device that calls an API endpoint, and SDKs that send information, are 'gaining access' (paras 33-34). Information used only inside the device is not access until it, or anything derived from it, leaves (para 44). IP addresses can trigger 5(3) (paras 54-55). Exemptions are not analysed and must be assessed case by case (para 56).

Art. 5(3) has two exemptions, as WP29 Opinion 04/2012 (WP194) quotes them: storage or access 'for the sole purpose of carrying out the transmission of a communication', or 'strictly necessary in order for the provider of an information society service explicitly requested by the subscriber or user to provide the service'. WP194 concludes that first-party analytics are 'not exempt from consent but pose limited privacy risks', because the user can use every function without them. Inference: crash and usage reporting in Rouxtine is not strictly necessary either, so it needs consent, which the owner's opt-in already gives. EUR-Lex itself returned an empty 202 bot challenge through the proxy.

EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent (v1.1). Pre-ticked opt-in boxes are invalid. Consent must be granular, separate for each purpose. Withdrawal must work through the same interface where consent was given, free of charge and without lowering service levels (GDPR art. 7(3)).

GDPR art. 8 (EDPB 05/2020 §7.1): when processing rests on consent and an information society service is offered directly to a child, a child under 16 needs consent given or authorised by a parent. Member states may lower the age, but not below 13, and a cross-border service may have to follow each country's age. The controller must make 'reasonable efforts' to verify. Art. 8 does not apply if the service is clearly offered only to people aged 18 or over. Inference: speedcubing has many young users, so this applies to Rouxtine whenever the data sent is personal (IP address, persistent ID).

Play Families policy: if a declared target audience includes children, the app must not transmit AAID, SIM serial, build serial, BSSID, MAC, SSID, IMEI or IMSI from children or users of unknown age. Mixed-audience apps 'must not implement APIs or SDKs that are not approved for use in child-directed services' unless the SDK runs behind a neutral age screen or collects no children's data. The Families self-certified SDK list applies to ads SDKs only, so zero ads means no list requirement.

Measured minSdk of every candidate SDK is at or below Rouxtine's 24: ACRA 14, Bugsnag 16, Aptabase 16, Sentry 21, Countly 21, PostHog 23, TelemetryDeck 23, Firebase measurement 24. options.name: A. Vitals + Sentry SaaS EU (crashes) + PostHog EU via an in-house client (usage stats), same in both flavours
options.summary: Play adds Android vitals on top. Both flavours ship sentry-android-core 8.62.0 with auto-init off, starting only after consent and reporting to a Sentry organisation in the EU region (Frankfurt) on the free Developer plan. Usage stats go to PostHog Cloud EU through a small Kotlin client (Room queue + WorkManager, '$process_person_profile': false), not the PostHog SDK. The DSN and PostHog key are committed (both public by design).
pros: Mature Android crash tooling: ANR detection, R8 mapping upload, release health, a 30-envelope offline disk cache
Free tiers fit an opt-in app: 5k errors and 1M events a month
EU storage for event data in both services
The SDKs are MIT and the usage client is Rouxtine's own GPL code, so F-Droid allows both. Opt-in avoids the Tracking label, with Element X and AnkiDroid as precedents
One code path and one dashboard per concern in both flavours
The in-house client adds no OkHttp or Gson (the PostHog SDK would add about 2.6 MB of artifacts) and gives full control over what leaves the device
cons: Two processors, so two DPAs and two privacy-policy entries
Sentry's server is FSL (source-available), with a small reviewer-discretion risk of an F-Droid NonFreeNet label
Sentry keeps account and project metadata in the US
Sentry's 1-user and 5k-error caps; the usage client (about 200 lines) must be built and tested

options.name: B. Vitals + PostHog only (SDK with error tracking + analytics)
options.summary: One vendor and one SDK (posthog-android 3.73.1, minSdk 23) for both exceptions (100k a month free) and usage events (1M a month free) in PostHog Cloud EU.
pros: One processor, one DPA, one dashboard
Most generous free tier; usage stops at the limit instead of billing
MIT SDK and a mostly MIT server; EU in Frankfurt with IP capture off by default
cons: Android crash support is basic: uncaught exceptions only; the docs mention no ANR or native crashes, and whether crashes persist across restarts is undocumented
About 2.6 MB of added artifacts before R8 (OkHttp, Gson, Okio)
Lifecycle autocapture is on by default and must be turned off for data minimisation

options.name: C. Vitals + ACRA with user-sent reports only (NewPipe pattern), no usage analytics
options.summary: acra-core (Apache-2.0, minSdk 14, about 0.3 MB) saves crash reports on the device. On the next launch the user sees the report and can open a pre-filled GitHub issue, email it, copy it, or dismiss it. Nothing is sent automatically.
pros: Zero third parties, zero cost, no server, no DPA
Nothing leaves the device without an explicit tap per report, the cleanest position under art. 5(3) and F-Droid's rules
Precedents: NewPipe and AnkiDroid ship ACRA on F-Droid without anti-features
Smallest footprint
cons: Few reports arrive: GitHub needs an account, and email exposes the reporter's address (personal data the owner then holds)
No ANRs, no aggregation or crash-free rates, manual R8 retrace
No usage analytics at all, so it doesn't meet the owner's 'improve the app' goal

options.name: D. Option A with GlitchTip hosted EU instead of Sentry SaaS
options.summary: Same Sentry Android SDK, with the DSN pointing at GlitchTip's hosted EU (Germany) free plan: 1,000 events a month, 30 days. The server is MIT, Sentry-compatible, and self-hostable on a 512 MB VM later.
pros: Fully FOSS backend, which settles the NonFreeNet question for F-Droid
Swapping in only changes the DSN; the code is identical
EU hosting; an upgrade costs only $15 a month
cons: 1,000 events a month is tight if a release crash-loops; events past the cap are lost
R8/ProGuard deobfuscation has open bugs (#504, #413, #519), so it needs -dontobfuscate or manual retrace
A smaller project, with fewer features than Sentry (ANR grouping, release health)

pros: No cost, no event caps for Crashlytics, rich dashboards
Built-in opt-in switch and local storage while off
cons: Closed: play-services-* under the Android SDK License needs onionhoney's GPL s.7 permission, the same blocker as Play Billing
Analytics merges the AD_ID and ACCESS_ADSERVICES_AD_ID permissions and pulls play-services-ads-identifier, against 'no advertising ID'
No EU data residency (any Google facility)
Forbidden in F-Droid, so the foss flavour gets nothing and the two flavours diverge
Contradicts the owner's 'open-source SDK where possible'

options.name: F. TelemetryDeck, Aptabase, Countly or Bugsnag
options.summary: Other candidates, each considered and ruled out.
pros: TelemetryDeck: German company, double-hashed IDs, disk cache
Aptabase: AGPL server, EU region
Countly: MIT SDK with a persisted queue
Bugsnag: MIT SDK, 32-event disk cache
cons: TelemetryDeck: backend not shown to be open source, free tier cut to 50k for new accounts, heaviest SDK (Ktor + AppCompat), a US host among its providers
Aptabase: no offline queue (fails offline-first), SDK only on JitPack, no crash reports
Countly: no free hosted tier ($175 a month) and Lite needs a server
Bugsnag: proprietary SaaS, 7-day free retention, EU residency unconfirmed, bundled native root-detection library

recommendation:
Recommend option A, with option D's GlitchTip as a ready fallback. Firebase (E) is ruled out: closed, needs onionhoney's s.7 permission, adds AD_ID permissions, and has no EU residency.

PLAY FLAVOUR
1. Android vitals is always on. It needs no SDK and no consent, and Google collects it under the user's own opt-in. It covers Play installs only.
2. Crash reports: io.sentry:sentry-android-core 8.62.0 only (no NDK, replay or performance), reporting to a new Sentry organisation created in the EU region (Frankfurt), free Developer plan.
   - Manifest `io.sentry.auto-init=false`. Call SentryAndroid.init only when crash reporting is allowed.
   - Settings: dataCollection.userInfo=false, enableAutoSessionTracking=false (or keep sessions if crash-free rates are wanted), attachScreenshot and attachViewHierarchy false, plus a beforeSend that drops the user and installation ID.
   - Project side: turn on 'prevent storing IP addresses' and add a scrubbing rule that removes geo.
   - Release builds use `-dontobfuscate` and keep line numbers. The source is public anyway, and this makes traces readable on any backend without uploading mappings.
3. Usage stats: a small in-house Kotlin client posting to PostHog Cloud EU's /batch/ endpoint (eu.i.posthog.com).
   - Events queue in Room and are sent by WorkManager with a network constraint, so it works offline-first.
   - Send few, aggregated events, such as module opened, session finished with duration bucket, and Rouxtine template used, with '$process_person_profile': false.
   - No persistent ID unless the owner wants retention metrics. If so, use a random ID that the user can reset.
   - In PostHog, keep IP capture off and turn GeoIP off.

FOSS FLAVOUR (GitHub/Obtainium, later F-Droid)
- The same code and the same backends. Both libraries are FLOSS from Maven Central or are Rouxtine's own code. Both features are opt-in and off by default, so F-Droid's Tracking label does not apply (the Element X and AnkiDroid precedents back this).
- Commit the DSN and the PostHog key: they are public by design, and F-Droid builds only include keys that are in the source.
- Keep the backend URLs in build config. If an F-Droid reviewer objects to sentry.io (FSL), switch the foss DSN to GlitchTip's hosted EU free plan without touching code.
- No Ko-fi or analytics differences beyond what HANDOFF already says.

CONSENT UX (identical in both flavours; run all text through the humanizer skill)
- Nothing leaves the device before consent. No SDK starts, nothing is queued for upload, and no ID is created.
- Crash reports have three choices: 'Ask me each time' (default), 'Always send', 'Never'.
  - Crashes are always written to a local file first. Data that stays on the device is outside art. 5(3) (EDPB 2/2023 para 44).
  - On the next launch, 'Ask me each time' shows a sheet: 'Rouxtine closed unexpectedly last time. Send the report?' with Send, Don't send, 'See what's sent' (the exact payload), and 'Always send'.
- Usage stats are a separate switch, off by default (EDPB 05/2020: granular, no pre-ticked boxes).
  - Offer it once on a 'Help improve Rouxtine' card after the user's first finished session, not on the first screen. 'No thanks' and 'Turn on' carry equal weight.
  - The card says what is sent, to whom (Sentry, PostHog), where (EU, Frankfurt), for how long, and links the privacy policy.
- Settings › Privacy holds the same controls. Turning one off takes effect at once (Sentry.close(), stop the worker), deletes queued events, and resets any ID (art. 7(3): withdrawal through the same interface).
- Store a local consent record: choices, timestamp, policy version. Ask again only if purposes change.
- Children: if the Play target audience includes under-16s, gate the usage-stats offer behind a neutral age question ('Are you 16 or older?') or make usage stats strictly non-personal. Then GDPR art. 8 and the Families SDK rule are covered.
- Debug and CI builds never send.
- Privacy policy on GitHub Pages: controller identity, the processors and their DPAs, data list, retention, and how to ask for deletion. Then fill the Data safety form:
  - Crash logs and Diagnostics: optional, not shared, Analytics.
  - App interactions: only with usage stats.
  - Device or other IDs: only if any ID is sent.
  - Location: none, once geo is scrubbed.
ownerQuestions: Which Play target-audience age groups will you declare? Do they include under-13s or under-16s? This decides whether usage stats need an age gate or must be fully non-personal (GDPR art. 8, Play Families policy).
Which EU country do you live in? It sets your lead data-protection authority and the national age of digital consent, which ranges from 13 to 16.

For crash reports, is Sentry's EU cloud (source-available FSL server, 5k errors a month free, mature R8 support) acceptable? Or do you want a fully open-source backend, GlitchTip EU (1k events a month free, deobfuscation still buggy), for both flavours or just foss?
Do you want usage analytics in R1, or crash reports first and usage stats later?
For usage stats, do you need retention numbers (a resettable random per-install ID, declared as 'Device or other IDs') or are anonymous aggregated events enough?
Are you OK publishing a privacy policy under your name with a contact email (on GitHub Pages), and signing the Sentry and PostHog data processing agreements as controller?
Is 'Ask me each time' an acceptable default for crash reports, so nothing is sent until the user taps? Or should crash reports simply be off until switched on?
Can release builds use -dontobfuscate (shrinking kept) so stack traces are readable without uploading mapping files?

issues.issue: The Rouxtine data model is underspecified, and two rules contradict each other. §3 says tuning inside a block 'carries forward silently', while §5 and scope say a saved Rouxtine never changes without consent. Neither doc says where that tuning is stored. There are also no stable block ids, which the rule 'show the note again at the next run' needs. Runs have no snapshot of the blocks they ran, and day variants have no structure. Follow-up blocks have no rule: 'Drill missed' / 'Drill slow' add a block to the run, so by §3's own rule ('blocks were added') every follow-up would trigger 'Update Rouxtine?'. issues.fix: Add a 'Data model' subsection to rouxtine-design.md §3. (1) Rouxtine {id UUID, originId, revision, formatVersion, name, description, level, goals, provenance, archivedAt}. Variant {id, name, order}; a Rouxtine without variants has one implicit variant. Block {id UUID stable across revisions, variantId, order, module, moduleVersion, mode, settings, selector, stop, role, description}. (2) Each saved edit creates a new revision, and RouxtineRevision keeps the JSON snapshot. (3) Run {id, rouxtineId?, rouxtineRevision, variantId?, status, dayKey}. RunBlock {id, runId, sourceBlockId?, blockSnapshot JSON, kind = planned | followUp | quick, status = done | skipped | partial, note, rating}. Notes come back by sourceBlockId. (4) Adaptive state (ladder level, bootstrap progress, case weights, metronome tempo) is never stored in the Rouxtine. It is derived from the attempt log, keyed by (module, mode, case-pool signature). It then carries forward without touching the saved Rouxtine and is shared when the same drill appears in two Rouxtines. (5) A structural change is any block added, removed, reordered or swapped, or a user edit to a block's settings, selector or stop rule during the run. Follow-up blocks and skips are not structural. (6) Deleting a Rouxtine archives it, and its runs keep their snapshots.

issues.issue: Sharing has no wire format, no size limits and no intake path. The doc names neither the encoding nor the checksum, and sets no cap on the text code or the QR. Nothing protects import from untrusted input; a pasted code can be a decompression bomb. QR scanning is unplanned: Google's code scanner runs in Play services, so it can't ship in the `foss` build. File import is unplanned too: a `.rouxtine` intent filter does not match reliably, because path attributes need a scheme and host, and file managers hand out content:// URIs with opaque paths. Measured on a realistic 7-block A/B Rouxtine with descriptions: 2,241 B of JSON → 839 B raw deflate → a 1,124-character `RXT1.` base64url code → QR version 27 at ECC M (125×125 modules), or version 24 at L. Version 40-M holds at most 2,331 bytes.
issues.evidence: Measured with segno 1.6.1 in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/7854d768-c194-5c37-87d5-37b386887809/scratchpad/audit/sizing.py. 50 MB of zeros deflates to 48,604 bytes (64,808 base64 characters). ML Kit code scanner docs: works 'without requiring your app to request camera permission' by 'delegating the task of scanning the code to Google Play services'. Android <data> docs: path attributes 'are meaningful only if the scheme and host attributes are also specified'. training-regimens.md:423 (Monkeytype warns above 2,000 characters).
issues.fix: Specify the following in §7. (1) Code = `RXT1.` + base64url(raw DEFLATE(UTF-8 JSON payload)) + `.` + base64url(CRC-32 of the JSON). The importer finds the `RXT<n>.` token inside surrounding text and strips whitespace and line breaks. (2) Caps: name ≤ 60 chars, description ≤ 280, block description ≤ 140, ≤ 4 variants, ≤ 12 blocks per variant. Settings are encoded as a diff from the module's defaults. The text code is ≤ 2,000 chars, which keeps the QR at or below about version 35-M. Above the cap, the QR option is hidden with a reason, and text and file still work. (3) Untrusted input: inflate with a hard output cap (64 KiB), refuse files over 256 KiB before reading, and run a lenient decoder that range-checks every field and never crashes past the preview screen. (4) Make the QR with ZXing core (Apache-2.0) in both flavours, in byte mode, holding the same text code. Scan with CameraX + ZXing (both FOSS), asking for CAMERA only at use. Also add 'Import from image', which decodes a QR from a screenshot chosen with the photo picker, because QR codes travel as images in chats. (5) The file holds the text code. Accept ACTION_SEND (text/plain, */*) and ACTION_VIEW (*/*) and sniff the `RXT` prefix. Make the in-app 'Import from file' (ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT) the documented path, and add 'Paste code'.

The Ladder is underspecified: no step down (research proposes −1 under 40 %), no per-module bounds, no starting level, and no plan for sampling a random state at an exact optimal length, which is rare at short lengths (FB averages 6.21 moves). The 'Weakest' bootstrap unit and whether it persists across runs are also unstated: 3 successes per case × angle over 42 CMLL × 4 is 504 reps.

issues.fix: Add 'Selector rules' to §5. An empty pool means the block can't start; the builder flags it, and a run offers 'edit filter' or 'skip'. N = 1 repeats the case with cooldown 0. Coverage counts cases; the module decides whether angles count. `reps` counts completed attempts, including DNF and excluding abort and `interrupted`. Stop rules are checked between attempts, so `time(T)` lets the current attempt finish. Ladder: +1 at ≥ 80 % optimal over the last 10, −1 under 40 %, bounds declared per module (wodzik's ranges as defaults). The starting level is the last level in the log for the same (module, mode, pool) signature, otherwise the module default. Sampling uses a depth-indexed sampler from the solver's pruning tables, with a retry budget; it falls back to the nearest length and logs the length actually served. Weakest: bootstrap per case × angle for recognition modes and per case for execution modes. Bootstrap state is derived from the log, so it spans runs, and it applies only to the active pool (design-9). Realistic: natural probabilities per case set, precomputed from the random-state generator and versioned with the set.

ownerQuestions.question: Write to onionhoney now? As a public GitHub issue, an email to the address on their commits, or both, and under which name?
ownerQuestions.why: Play Billing (and any closed Google library) cannot ship next to their GPL code without their written s.7 permission (play-billing-gpl.md). Upstream has been quiet since 2025-07-27, so a reply may be slow, and a 'no' changes the money plan.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Ask now, as a public issue on onionhoney/roux-trainers (it leaves a written record), optionally pointed to by email, under your own name. Use the draft in play-billing-gpl.md §9 and offer a PR that adds the licence line and the permission to their README. Don't block on the answer.

ownerQuestions.question: What should the letter ask for: Play Billing only, every Google Play/Play services/Firebase library, an app-store (Play terms) permission, and consent to name 'Roux Trainers'/onionhoney in the listing?
ownerQuestions.why: A wider ask keeps Crashlytics, ML Kit and in-app review open later but is less likely to get a yes. Play's terms against the GPL's no-further-restrictions clause affect every Play build. Naming them in the listing needs consent.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Ask for the narrow Play Billing permission as drafted, plus a Terpoir-style app-store permission and consent to name them in the listing. Skip the wider library wording: R1 needs none of those libraries.

ownerQuestions.question: If onionhoney says no or never answers, do you accept a separate paid 'Supporter key' app (no billing library) as the way to sell themes, or no paid extras on Play at all?
ownerQuestions.why: Without the permission, in-app purchases are impossible, but a paid download needs no library and nobody's permission.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Accept the paid Supporter key app (option d1) and never ship Play Billing in that case.

ownerQuestions.question: Do you want to offer onionhoney anything beyond credit (revenue share, a free Supporter unlock)?
ownerQuestions.why: It is their code, and the ask comes from someone who will charge for cosmetics next to it.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Credit them in the app, the listing and every ported file, and give them the Supporter unlock for free. Leave a revenue share for them to raise.

ownerQuestions.question: What may the 'paid smart-cube add-on' contain?
ownerQuestions.why: Every smart-cube feature in scope is a trainer input, a module (SC), stats (automatic splits) or analysis, which 'never paywall a trainer, stats or analysis' forbids. monetization.md's candidates were all analytics. As written, no smart-cube feature can be both paid and compliant.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Keep protocols, the SC module, automatic splits, smart-cube input and all smart-cube stats free in both builds. Drop the add-on, or limit it to cosmetic extras (cube skins, replay themes), so the Supporter themes stay the paid item.

ownerQuestions.question: Contributor and template terms, and Weblate timing: is it OK to make contributions GPL-3.0-only plus the Play s.7 permission plus a DCO sign-off from the first commit? Which licence for community templates? Start Weblate when the first screens exist (HANDOFF) or once R1 strings settle (scope)?
ownerQuestions.why: Every outside contributor, template author or translator is another copyright holder who would have to agree to the Play permission later. The two docs disagree on when Weblate starts.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Code and translations: GPL-3.0-only with DCO plus the same s.7 permission, from the first commit. Templates: CC0-1.0. Weblate: once R1 strings settle.

ownerQuestions.question: Keep R1 free of closed Google libraries (Firebase, ML Kit/code scanner, Play Core review/update, oss-licenses) even if onionhoney's permission arrives in time?
ownerQuestions.why: Until a permission covers them they are barred anyway. Keeping them out makes R1 independent of the answer and keeps the foss build F-Droid-clean.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Yes. Use FLOSS reporting, ZXing for QR, AboutLibraries for licences, and no Play Core prompts.

ownerQuestions.question: min2phase: rely on Chen Shuang's 2023 MIT section in the README, or also ask Chen to confirm it covers the GPL-headed Search.java?
ownerQuestions.why: The README's MIT section and Search.java's GPL-3.0-or-later header disagree.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Port the Java under the MIT grant and send Chen a one-line confirmation request. Don't wait on it.

ownerQuestions.question: EU Cyber Resilience Act: will you get a short legal opinion before selling anything?
ownerQuestions.why: Selling an unlock probably makes Rouxtine a product in a commercial activity. Manufacturer duties apply from 2027-12-11 (SBOM, vulnerability handling, five-year support, declaration of conformity), and exploited-vulnerability reporting has applied since 2026-09-11. Donations alone don't count.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Keep R1 and the foss build free of any sale. Get a legal opinion before scope item 11. If the CRA applies, budget the work or keep money to off-Play donations.

ownerQuestions.question: Trader status: declare non-trader while nothing is sold? And are you OK with Play showing your phone number (from 2027-03-01) as well as your address once you become a trader?
ownerQuestions.why: Every Play account must declare trader or non-trader status at creation. You accepted the public address, but the phone number is new (verified on Play help 17594752).
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Declare non-trader while nothing is sold on Play, if your own assessment agrees. Switch before the first paid product, once the phone number is acceptable.

ownerQuestions.question: Ko-fi scope: README only ('Ko-fi on GitHub only'), or README plus the foss app plus F-Droid metadata as HANDOFF reads it? Add a FUNDING.yml Sponsor button?
ownerQuestions.why: HANDOFF widened your 'GitHub only'. The README has no Ko-fi line yet, and no to-do covered the Ko-fi page.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Keep the wider reading (all three are off Play). Add the README line once the Ko-fi page exists. FUNDING.yml is optional and changes nothing for Play, because the play build never links to the repo page.

ownerQuestions.question: Crash and usage tools: is option A acceptable? That is Android vitals, plus sentry-android-core to Sentry's EU region on the free plan, plus a small in-house client posting anonymous events to PostHog Cloud EU, in both flavours. Or do you want GlitchTip's fully open-source backend?
ownerQuestions.why: HANDOFF left the tool open. Firebase is ruled out: it is closed, needs onionhoney's permission, is banned on F-Droid and adds AD_ID. Sentry's server is source-available (FSL), not FLOSS.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Option A, with GlitchTip EU as the drop-in fallback (only the DSN changes), for example if an F-Droid reviewer objects.

ownerQuestions.question: Which Play target-audience age groups will you declare, and which EU country do you live in?
ownerQuestions.why: If under-16s are in the audience, GDPR art. 8 and Play's Families mixed-audience rule apply to any reporting SDK. The country sets the age of digital consent (13-16) and your data-protection authority. Outside the EEA, an art. 27 representative may be needed. Texas app-store age-signal law may also apply.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Declare 13-15, 16-17 and 18+ (not under 13). Put a neutral age picker, not a leading 'Are you 16 or older?', before the reporting offers, and offer reporting only from 16 (or your country's age). Younger users get Android vitals only.

ownerQuestions.question: Crash-report default: 'Ask me after a crash' (local file, a sheet on the next launch), or off until switched on in Settings?
ownerQuestions.why: Both are consent-compliant. 'Ask' gets more reports without sending anything silently.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: 'Ask me after a crash', with Sentry not started in that mode.

ownerQuestions.question: Usage stats in R1, or crash reports first and usage stats later?
ownerQuestions.why: Scope puts both in R1. Usage stats add a privacy-policy entry, a Data safety entry and a consent card.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Keep both in R1 as scoped, and build crash reports first.

ownerQuestions.question: Do you need retention numbers, which require a stored, resettable random ID declared as 'Device or other IDs', or are anonymous aggregated events enough?
ownerQuestions.why: A persistent ID makes the data more personal and adds a Data safety entry.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: No ID: anonymous events only.

ownerQuestions.question: Are you OK publishing a privacy policy under your name with a contact email (on nauroth.github.io) and accepting Sentry's and PostHog's processing terms as data controller?
ownerQuestions.why: Play requires a privacy policy for every app, even one collecting nothing, to complete the Data safety form. Opt-in reporting makes you a controller.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Yes, on nauroth.github.io, with no Ko-fi on that site.

ownerQuestions.question: May release builds use -dontobfuscate (R8 shrinking kept), so stack traces are readable without uploading mapping files?
ownerQuestions.why: The source is public anyway, and it avoids GlitchTip's deobfuscation bugs and mapping uploads that eat into its quota.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Yes.

ownerQuestions.question: Your Q17: '.apk on GitHub should be enough no? Or publish on Obtainium and F-Droid also?'
ownerQuestions.why: Obtainium is not a store: it reads GitHub releases, so there is nothing to publish. The F-Droid main repo signs with its own key unless the build is reproducible, which breaks switching between builds. HANDOFF had recorded 'F-Droid later' as if confirmed.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: R1: Play plus the GitHub APK. After R1, IzzyOnDroid first (it ships our own signed APK). The F-Droid main repo only with reproducible builds. Keep foss F-Droid-clean from day one.

ownerQuestions.question: When should the Play closed test start?
ownerQuestions.why: The 14 consecutive days with 12 opted-in testers, plus up to 7 days of review, sit on R1's critical path after a 41-item scope.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Open it at milestone M5 with 15-20 testers, so the test and the review overlap the last milestone. No public release before R1.

ownerQuestions.question: Daily streak plus weekly goal: is the 'flexible rest days' rule OK?
ownerQuestions.why: With the default 3-day goal, a user who meets it misses four days a week. Unless those are rest days, the streak breaks every week, which contradicts 'no punishment for breaks'.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: A missed day counts as a rest day while the week can still reach its goal. Freezes cover the rest (one earned per week the goal is met, at most 2 banked). Fixed rest weekdays are an option (rouxtine-design.md §8).

ownerQuestions.question: Backup and moving to a new phone: include Android Auto Backup and a manual export/import in R1?
ownerQuestions.why: There are no accounts or server, so all history, SRS state and Rouxtines live only on the phone. Auto Backup silently stops above 25 MB, and the Twisty/Cubic export carries times only.
ownerQuestions.recommendation: Both in R1. Configure Auto Backup to keep only the source-of-truth tables and rebuild caches after a restore, and add a manual 'Export all data' / 'Import data' zip via the Storage Access Framework. No cloud sync.
